response: ## The finding `crime_00041` — **Oversized Raster**, `src/assets/hero-banner.png`, confidence 0.95: > "byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB)" > "severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB" > "format: png" ## Verdict: request changes, don't block 253.9 KB lands in the **low** band — 27% over the 200 KB floor, nowhere near the 500 KB medium bar. Aggregate risk agrees: `agent_risk` 0.14, the second-lowest of all 42 findings. Nothing here justifies a red X on a landing-page PR. Two things push it above "nit" though: 1. **It's the hero.** A landing-page hero is almost always the LCP element, so this is the single asset on the site where 254 KB has a direct, measurable Core Web Vitals cost. Same byte count in a docs page footer would be a shrug. 2. **`effort: quick`.** The fix is a re-export, not a refactor. There's no good reason to merge it and file a follow-up. So: request changes, expect a new commit in the same PR, re-review takes 30 seconds. One caveat on the evidence — the finding reports bytes but **not pixel dimensions** for this detector (contrast `crime_00038`, which gives "32 × 32 px"). So I can't tell you the overdraw ratio from the scan alone. Check the intrinsic size before re-encoding; if it's a 4000px-wide export rendering into a 1200px slot, the resize alone does most of the work. ## The actual smell: it's a PNG A 254 KB PNG hero is usually one of two mistakes, and which one it is changes the fix: - **A photograph exported as PNG.** PNG has no lossy mode, so a photo pays full price for every pixel. This is the common case and the resize + re-encode below fixes it outright. - **A flat illustration or gradient at 2–3× the needed resolution.** Here the resize is the whole win; the format change is secondary. ## Recommended transformation **Dimensions.** Size to the widest CSS px the hero actually renders at, times 2 for HiDPI, and cap there. For a typical full-bleed hero on a 1280–1440px max-width layout: ```html ``` 2560px is the ceiling — that's 2× a 1280 layout and covers every retina laptop. Anything above that is bytes nobody sees. Keep `width`/`height` on the `` so it doesn't contribute CLS, and `fetchpriority="high"` since it's the LCP candidate. **Format: AVIF, with WebP as the fallback source.** Reasons, in order of weight: - On photographic content AVIF typically runs **30–50% smaller than WebP** at visually equivalent quality. On a hero that's the difference between ~90 KB and ~50 KB. - AVIF handles **large smooth gradients** without the banding WebP shows — heroes are mostly sky, blur, and brand-color washes, which is exactly WebP's weak spot. - Browser support is no longer a reason to hesitate (Chrome 85+, Firefox 93+, Safari 16.4+). The `` WebP source covers the tail without costing modern browsers anything. Two places I'd flip that call: if the hero is a **flat vector-style illustration with hard edges and few colors**, lossless WebP often beats AVIF and encodes far faster — and you should ask whether it wants to be an SVG at all. And if the build is latency-sensitive, note AVIF encoding is genuinely slow; that's fine at build time, painful in a request path. **Budget.** Target **≤ 100 KB** for the delivered LCP variant, and expect ~40–60 KB from AVIF at q50–60 once the resize is applied. Worth encoding as an actual CI check so the next hero doesn't rediscover this. ## Not this PR's problem, but worth a comment The same `src/assets/` directory has two pre-existing asset findings the author didn't introduce: `crime_00034` (`partner-logo.svg` carries two base64 rasters — **high** severity, an SVG that isn't really vector) and `crime_00038` (`check-icon.png` at 32×32, which should be SVG). If they're already in the image-pipeline headspace, that's a natural follow-up ticket — but don't gate this PR on it.
